Reusable Button (Variants & Sizes)
learnings.answer:
A **reusable Button** with **variants** (primary, secondary, ghost) and **sizes** (sm, md, lg) mirrors design systems like MUI. The goal is a small API surface, consistent styling, and composability — without duplicating CSS everywhere.

## API design

```javascript
<Button variant="primary" size="md" disabled={false} onClick={handleClick}>
  Save
</Button>;
```

| Prop | Type | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `variant` | `'primary' \| 'secondary' \| 'ghost'` | Visual style |
| `size` | `'sm' \| 'md' \| 'lg'` | Padding, font-size |
| `disabled` | boolean | Blocks interaction |
| `as` | element type | Polymorphic render (`'a'`, `Link`) |

## Variant map pattern (MUI/cva style)

```javascript
const variantStyles = {
  primary: "bg-blue-600 text-white hover:bg-blue-700",
  secondary: "bg-gray-200 text-gray-900 hover:bg-gray-300",
  ghost: "bg-transparent text-blue-600 hover:bg-blue-50",
};

const sizeStyles = {
  sm: "px-3 py-1 text-sm",
  md: "px-4 py-2 text-base",
  lg: "px-6 py-3 text-lg",
};

function Button({
  variant = "primary",
  size = "md",
  as: Component = "button",
  className = "",
  disabled,
  children,
  ...props
}) {
  const classes = [
    "inline-flex items-center justify-center rounded font-medium",
    "focus-visible:outline focus-visible:outline-2",
    "disabled:opacity-50 disabled:pointer-events-none",
    variantStyles[variant],
    sizeStyles[size],
    className,
  ].join(" ");

  return (
    <Component className={classes} disabled={disabled} {...props}>
      {children}
    </Component>
  );
}
```

## How to answer in the interview

> "I'd define variant and size as enums mapped to class names or tokens, default props for md/primary, forward ref and rest props for flexibility, and support polymorphic `as` for links. Disabled state uses opacity and pointer-events-none."

## Common mistakes

- Hardcoding colors in every usage instead of tokens
- Not forwarding `ref` (needed for focus management)
- Using `<div onClick>` instead of `<button>` for actions (a11y)

## Key takeaways

- **Variant maps** keep styling DRY and scalable.
- Always use semantic `<button>` unless `as` provides an accessible alternative.
- Spread `...props` for `onClick`, `type`, `aria-*` extensibility.

## Interview follow-ups

- **Loading state?** — `isLoading` prop swaps children for spinner, sets `aria-busy`.
- **Icon buttons?** — `startIcon` / `endIcon` slots or children composition.

learnings.title: Class Lifecycle, Hooks & Reconciliation
learnings.answer:
React components go through **mount → update → unmount** phases. **Hooks** replaced most class lifecycle methods with composable functions. **Reconciliation** is React's diffing algorithm that decides what actually changes in the DOM.

## Class lifecycle (legacy but still asked)

| Phase | Methods | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mount | `constructor`, `render`, `componentDidMount` | Initial render + side effects |
| Update | `render`, `componentDidUpdate` | Re-render after props/state change |
| Unmount | `componentWillUnmount` | Cleanup timers, subscriptions |

## Hooks equivalents

| Class | Hooks |
| --- | --- |
| `componentDidMount` | `useEffect(() => { ... }, [])` |
| `componentDidUpdate` | `useEffect(() => { ... }, [dep])` |
| `componentWillUnmount` | `useEffect(() => () => cleanup(), [])` |
| `this.state` | `useState` |
| Context | `useContext` |

**Rules of Hooks:** only call at top level; only in React functions.

## Reconciliation

Think of reconciliation as **diffing two versions of a UI tree** — like comparing two shopping lists and only buying what changed.

1. React builds a **virtual DOM** (element tree).
2. On state change, it builds a new tree and **diffs** against the previous.
3. It computes the minimal DOM updates (**commit** phase).

**Reconciliation heuristics** (see [GreatFrontEnd](https://www.greatfrontend.com/questions/quiz/what-is-reconciliation-in-react)):

| Comparison | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Different element type | Tear down old subtree, build new |
| Same element type | Update props in place |
| Same position, different `key` | Treat as different items |
| List items | `key` gives stable identity across reorders |

**Keys** help React match list items across renders — use **stable unique ids**, not index when list reorders.

```javascript
// Bad: index key when list reorders
items.map((item, i) => <Row key={i} data={item} />);

// Good: stable id
items.map((item) => <Row key={item.id} data={item} />);
```



## Effect order on mount and update

On every render, React runs in this order:

1. **Render** — call component function, build virtual tree
2. **Commit** — apply DOM mutations
3. **useLayoutEffect** — runs synchronously after DOM updates, **before** the browser paints
4. **Browser paint**
5. **useEffect** — runs asynchronously after paint

On **update** when dependencies change:

1. Cleanup from the previous effect runs first (with the **old** closure values)
2. New effect runs with updated values

```javascript
useEffect(() => {
  console.log('effect', count);
  return () => console.log('cleanup', count);
}, [count]);
// count 0→1 logs: "cleanup 0", then "effect 1"
```

On **unmount**, all effect cleanups run once.

## Batching

React 18 **automatically batches** multiple `setState` calls in event handlers, promises, and timeouts into one re-render.

## How to answer in the interview

> "Lifecycle is mount, update, unmount. Hooks map DidMount/DidUpdate/WillUnmount to useEffect with dependency arrays. Reconciliation diffs virtual trees; keys identify list nodes. React batches updates for performance."

## Common mistakes

- Missing dependency array → infinite `useEffect` loops
- Using index as key for sortable/filterable lists
- Putting side effects directly in render instead of `useEffect`

## Key takeaways

- Hooks = composable lifecycle + state; respect the rules.
- Reconciliation minimizes real DOM work via diffing + keys.
- React 18 batches updates broadly for fewer paints.

## Interview follow-ups

- **useLayoutEffect vs useEffect?** — Layout runs synchronously after DOM mutations, before paint.
- **What triggers re-render?** — State/props/context change in component or ancestor.

learnings.title: Big List Rendering (Virtualization)
learnings.answer:
**Virtualization** (windowing) renders only the **visible rows** (plus a small buffer) instead of thousands of DOM nodes. For large tables, feeds, and logs, it's the standard technique to keep scroll at 60fps and memory bounded. ## The problem Rendering 10,000 `
` rows means 10,000 DOM nodes, slow initial paint, and expensive reconciliation on updates. ## Windowing mental model Imagine a **sliding window** over your data array. Only items whose indices fall in `[startIndex, endIndex]` get mounted. As you scroll, the window moves — old nodes unmount, new ones mount. ``` Total items: 100,000 Viewport fits: ~20 rows Actually rendered: ~25 rows (with overscan buffer) ``` ## Fixed-height example (concept) ```javascript function VirtualList({ items, itemHeight, height }) { const [scrollTop, setScrollTop] = useState(0); const visibleCount = Math.ceil(height / itemHeight); const start = Math.floor(scrollTop / itemHeight); const end = start + visibleCount + 1; // overscan const slice = items.slice(start, end); return (
setScrollTop(e.target.scrollTop)} >
{slice.map((item, i) => (
{item}
))}
); } ``` ## Libraries | Library | Notes | | --- | --- | | `react-window` | Lightweight, fixed/variable size lists and grids | | `react-virtualized` | Older, more features, heavier | | `@tanstack/react-virtual` | Headless, flexible | ## Tradeoffs | Fixed height | Variable height | | --- | --- | | Simple math | Measure rows or estimate + correct | | Fast scroll | More complex, possible jank | ## How to answer in the interview > "I'd virtualize — compute visible range from scrollTop and row height, render only that slice inside a tall spacer container, add overscan for smooth scroll. For production I'd use react-window or TanStack Virtual. For variable heights I'd measure or use estimated sizes." ## Common mistakes - No overscan → blank flashes while scrolling fast - Wrong total scroll height → scrollbar jumps - Index as key when window shifts without stable item ids ## Key takeaways - Only mount visible items + small buffer. - Spacer div sets scroll height; inner list translates with `transform`. - Variable height needs measurement strategy. ## Interview follow-ups - **Infinite scroll + virtualization?** — Fetch next page when near end index. - **Accessibility?** — Ensure keyboard nav and screen reader range announcements.

When Does a Component Re-render?
learnings.answer:
A component **re-renders** when React needs to reconcile a new version of its output. Props changing alone does not schedule a render — something upstream must trigger it. ## Triggers | Trigger | Example | | --- | --- | | **Own state changes** | `setCount(1)`, `dispatch({ type: 'ADD' })` | | **Parent re-renders** | Parent state changes → all children render (unless memoized) | | **Context value changes** | Any consumer of a changed Provider re-renders | | **`forceUpdate`** | Class components only | | **Same state value** | React may bail out via `Object.is`, but still may render once | ## Does NOT trigger re-render | Action | Why | | --- | --- | | `ref.current = value` | Refs are mutable boxes outside React's render cycle | | Mutating state object in place | Same reference — React skips update | | Parent re-render with same props + `React.memo` | Shallow prop compare passes | ```javascript function Parent() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); return ( <> {/* re-renders every Parent click */} ); } const Child = React.memo(() =>
static
); // skips re-render ``` ## Key insight > Props don't cause re-renders — **parent re-renders** do. The child receives new props as a consequence. ## Key takeaways - State/context changes and parent renders are the main triggers. - `useRef` updates are invisible to React's scheduler. - `React.memo` prevents parent-driven re-renders when props are shallowly equal.

learnings.title: Preventing Context Re-renders
SSR, SSG, ISR & CSR
learnings.source: user paste: React interview concepts; interview-qa/03-nextjs.md
learnings.answer:
These are **rendering strategies** that decide where and when HTML is generated relative to the browser.

## Comparison

| Strategy | When rendered | Freshness | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **CSR** (Client-Side Rendering) | Browser after JS loads | Always client-fresh | Dashboards, authenticated apps |
| **SSR** (Server-Side Rendering) | Server on every request | Always fresh | Personalized, SEO-critical dynamic pages |
| **SSG** (Static Site Generation) | Build time | Stale until rebuild | Blogs, docs, marketing |
| **ISR** (Incremental Static Regeneration) | Build + background revalidate | Stale-while-revalidate | E-commerce, news with CDN scale |

## Mental model

```
CSR:  Browser downloads JS → renders empty shell → hydrates
SSR:  Server sends full HTML → browser hydrates → interactive
SSG:  HTML pre-built at deploy → CDN serves instantly
ISR:  SSG + periodic background rebuild (e.g. every 60s)
```

## Decision rule

- Default to **SSG/ISR** for public content (free CDN scale).
- Use **SSR** when data must be per-request (cookies, auth, live inventory).
- Use **CSR** for highly interactive post-login experiences where SEO doesn't matter.

## React 18 streaming SSR

Server can send HTML in **chunks** — critical content first, Suspense boundaries stream later. Improves TTFB and perceived performance.

## Key takeaways

- CSR = client renders; SSR/SSG/ISR = server (or build) sends HTML first.
- ISR is the sweet spot for content that changes occasionally.
- Hydration attaches React event listeners to server-rendered HTML.

learnings.title: Micro-frontend Architecture
learnings.source: user paste: React interview concepts; react-interview-prep.html
learnings.answer:
**Micro-frontends** decompose a large frontend into **independently deployable** apps that compose into one user-facing experience.

## Why teams adopt it

- Independent deploy cadence per team/domain
- Technology flexibility (different React versions — with care)
- Align team boundaries with business domains (checkout, catalog, account)

## Composition approaches

| Approach | Pros | Cons |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Module Federation** (Webpack 5) | Runtime sharing, shared deps | Build complexity, version skew |
| **iframes** | Strong isolation | Poor UX integration, routing pain |
| **Web Components** | Standards-based | Framework interop quirks |
| **Monorepo + packages** | Simpler ops | Coupled deploy unless careful |

## Module Federation sketch

```javascript
// Host webpack.config.js
new ModuleFederationPlugin({
  name: 'host',
  remotes: {
    checkout: 'checkout@http://localhost:3001/remoteEntry.js',
  },
  shared: { react: { singleton: true }, 'react-dom': { singleton: true } },
});

// Host component
const RemoteCart = React.lazy(() => import('checkout/Cart'));
```

## Common challenges

- **Shared state** — event bus, URL as source of truth, or lightweight global store
- **Routing** — host owns top-level routes; remotes own sub-routes
- **Consistent UX** — shared design tokens / component library
- **Dependency deduplication** — enforce single React instance via `shared` config

## Key takeaways

- Trade deployment independence for integration complexity.
- Module Federation is the most common React approach for runtime composition.
- Shared design system and routing contract are as important as the tech choice.
